places.quote: That fit has $\sigma_i^2 = \ln\!\big(1 + \text{s.e.}^2/\hat R_i^2\big)$, and its $z$-[[Percentile|percentile]] is $\hat R_i\exp(z\sigma_i - \sigma_i^2/2)$.
Its $p$-th percentile is then $R_p = e^{\mu + z_p\sigma}$.

requirements.statement: An empirical-limits confidence interval for ultimate loss applies the minimum and maximum observed individual age-to-age factors for each remaining development period (multiplying them across periods) to the latest cumulative loss to give the lower and upper bounds.

resolution.quote: the ultimate from the chain ladder with every remaining age-to-age factor replaced by the minimum, or the maximum, individual factor
resolution.note: Mack Chain Ladder Model (Mack printed p.133): empirical limits from the min/max observed individual factors

requirements.statement: An individual age-to-age factor is an accident year's cumulative loss at one age divided by its cumulative loss at the prior age.

places.quote: **Age-to-Age Factor** (link ratio) is the ratio of a cohort's cumulative amount at one maturity to its amount at the previous maturity

requirements.statement: A volume-weighted average age-to-age development factor is the sum of the later-age cumulative losses divided by the sum of the earlier-age cumulative losses, taken over the accident years that have both ages observed.

places.quote: **Volume-weighted average**: $\Sigma(\text{col }n{+}1) / \Sigma(\text{col }n)$ — gives more credibility to larger accident years; the standard default selection
f_{n \to n+1}^{\text{vol-wtd}} = \frac{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,n+1}}{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,n}}

requirements.statement: An age-to-ultimate development factor is the product of the successive age-to-age factors from that age through the last age, times the tail factor.

places.quote: \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \left(\prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1}\right) \times \text{Tail}

requirements.statement: In Sahasrabuddhe's method, to put a reported loss triangle on a basic-limit, latest-accident-year cost level, multiply each cell by the ratio of the basic-limit limited expected value (LEV) for the latest accident year at that age to the triangle-limit LEV for that cell's accident year at the same age.

places.quote: Restate each cell of the triangle, observed in layer $L$, to the basic limit at the latest cost level: $C^L_{i,j} \times LEV(B; \Phi_{n,j}) / LEV(L; \Phi_{i,j})$.

requirements.statement: Compute age-to-age and age-to-ultimate factors from the triangle adjusted to basic limit and latest cost level, using the volume-weighted averages and the given tail factor.

places.quote: \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \left(\prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1}\right) \times \text{Tail}

requirements.statement: To convert a basic-limit, current-cost-level age-to-ultimate factor to the triangle's limit and historical cost level, multiply it by the ratio of the triangle-limit to basic-limit LEV at the ultimate-age-minus-one (latest diagonal) age (for the latest year), divided by the same LEV ratio at the starting age; i.e., [LEV_limit(latest age)/LEV_basic(latest age)] / [LEV_limit(start age)/LEV_basic(start age)].

places.quote: \text{LDF}^L_t = \text{LDF}_t \times \frac{R^L}{R^L_t}

requirements.statement: The LEV ratios used in the final adjustment must come from the same accident year (the most recent, whose cost level is the target) across the relevant ages, not from other accident years.

The three components of internal systemic risk in a balanced scorecard assessment are specification error, parameter selection error, and data error, and each potential risk indicator is classified under one of them (e.g., predictor stability and number of models relate to specification error; best predictors identified relates to parameter selection; information from the business relates to data error).

places.quote: **Data error** comes from poor or unavailable data, or inadequate knowledge of the portfolio, including its pricing, underwriting and claims processes. Indicators include knowledge of past processes, information from the business, reconciliations, robust data processes, and past revisions of data.
**[[Internal Systemic Risk|Internal systemic risk]]** is specification error, parameter selection error and data error.
*Parameter selection error* is internal systemic risk, also called model specification risk (a [[Model Risk|model risk]]), and is potentially common across claim groups (see [[Risk Margin]]).

requirements.statement: In a balanced scorecard, a score of 1 is worst practice (highest risk) and 5 is best practice; a worst score for data information quality describes late, incomplete, inconsistent, unreliable or poorly documented information from the business.

places.quote: $s_r$ is risk indicator $r$'s score from $1$ to $5$ ($5$ is best practice)

requirements.statement: Compute a class's overall balanced scorecard score as the weighted average of its indicator scores, with each indicator weighted by the weight of the risk component it is assigned to (class-specific component weights).

places.quote: $$\bar s = \frac{\sum_r v_r\,s_r}{\sum_r v_r}$$

requirements.statement: Map each class's overall balanced scorecard score to a coefficient of variation using the lookup table of score ranges for that class.

places.quote: The CoV scale for this class (the paper's example scale for its long-tail CTP class) is $11.5\%$ for scores of $3.0$ to $3.5$ and $9.5\%$ for $3.5$ to $4.0$.

requirements.statement: Total internal systemic risk CoV across valuation classes = sqrt(Σi Σj ρij wi wj φi φj), where wi is the class's share of total outstanding liabilities, φi its CoV, and ρ the correlation between classes (for two classes: w1²φ1² + w2²φ2² + 2ρw1w2φ1φ2 under the root).
requirements.concept: Risk Margin Aggregation (Independent, Internal and External Systemic Risk)

places.quote: $$\mathrm{CoV}_{\text{int}} = \frac{\sqrt{\sum_i\sum_j \rho_{ij}\,(w_i c_i)(w_j c_j)}}{\sum_i w_i}$$

requirements.statement: Total CoV of insurance liabilities = sqrt(independent CoV² + internal systemic CoV² + external systemic CoV²), because the three risk sources are treated as independent of each other.
requirements.concept: Risk Margin Aggregation (Independent, Internal and External Systemic Risk)

places.quote: There are no cross terms, because independent risk is uncorrelated with every other source of uncertainty and between valuation portfolios.
The categories are chosen so that they are independent of each other, so there are no cross terms.
The three sources are taken as independent, so $\mathrm{CoV}^2 = \mathrm{CoV}_{\text{ind}}^2 + \mathrm{CoV}_{\text{int}}^2 + \mathrm{CoV}_{\text{ext}}^2$.

requirements.statement: For a Normal distribution of liabilities, risk margin = z × CoV × mean, where z is the standard normal percentile for the required probability of adequacy and mean is the total outstanding claims liability (central estimate).

places.quote: Under a normal distribution the margin is $z_p \times \mathrm{CoV} \times$ the central estimate.

requirements.statement: The unlimited age-to-ultimate loss development factor is the product of the unlimited age-to-age factors from the current age through the tail factor.

places.quote: \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \left(\prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1}\right) \times \text{Tail}
CDFs are built **backwards from the tail**: start with the tail factor, multiply in each successive age-to-age factor moving toward younger ages.

requirements.statement: Siewert's method: the limited LDF at a given limit from age t to ultimate equals the unlimited LDF times the ratio of the limited severity relativity at ultimate to that at age t (R_ult / R_t).

places.quote: \text{LDF}^L_t = \text{LDF}_t \times \frac{R^L}{R^L_t}

requirements.statement: The limited severity relativity for a layer between a lower and an upper limit is the ratio of the limited severity at the lower limit to the limited severity at the upper limit, at a given maturity.

places.quote: For a layer between two limits, the relativity becomes a difference, $(R^{L_2} - R^{L_1})/(R^{L_2}_t - R^{L_1}_t)$.

requirements.statement: Siewert's excess layer LDF equals the LDF limited to the upper limit times (1 − ultimate layer relativity) / (1 − layer relativity at age t), where the relativity is lower-limit severity over upper-limit severity.

places.quote: \text{XSLDF}^L_t = \text{LDF}_t \times \frac{1 - R^L}{1 - R^L_t}

requirements.statement: Reported loss in a layer between two limits equals reported loss limited to the upper limit minus reported loss limited to the lower limit.
requirements.concept: Limited Losses and Layers of Loss

places.quote: X_{(a,b]} = \min(X, b) - \min(X, a)
E[Y] = E[X \wedge (R + L)] - E[X \wedge R]

requirements.statement: In the direct development approach, IBNR for a layer equals the layer's reported loss times (layer LDF − 1), applying the layer LDF directly to the layer's reported losses.
requirements.concept: Direct Development Approach for Layer IBNR

places.quote: **Direct development** applies an [[Excess Loss Development Factor|excess loss development factor]] to reported excess losses.

requirements.statement: Strategic risk is the risk of failing to achieve business objectives from strategy choices, and includes types such as technology, reputation, competition, customer/intermediary, industry and stagnation risk, each distinct from project (execution) risk.

places.quote: **Strategic or [[Business Risk|business]] risk** — competition, the underwriting cycle, regulation, reputation, the wrong strategy.
**Strategic** risks come from reputational damage, competition, customer wants, demographic and social trends, technological innovation, capital availability, and regulatory and political trends.

requirements.statement: Primary causes of P&C insurer impairment and insolvency include deficient loss reserves, inadequate pricing, rapid growth, catastrophe events, reinsurance failure, external fraud, overstated assets, reckless management and insolvency of a subsidiary or affiliate.
The discount rate (cost of equity) is computed by CAPM as the risk-free rate plus beta times the equity market risk premium.

places.quote: $$k_E = r_f + \beta_E\,\bigl(E[r_m] - r_f\bigr)$$

resolution.quote: is the cost of equity by the capital asset pricing model
resolution.note: Cost of Capital (retagged) gives the CAPM cost of equity, risk-free rate plus beta times the market risk premium

requirements.statement: To value an acquisition target with transaction multiples, select comparable transactions with similar ROE, growth rate and discount rate, then multiply the target's book value (assets less liabilities, excluding intangible assets) by their price-to-book multiples to get a range of values.

In an ODP bootstrap, convert a sampled standardized Pearson residual into a sample incremental claim by inverting the residual formula (incremental = fitted + residual × sqrt(fitted)), then build the sampled triangle, calculate age-to-age factors from it, and project future incrementals.

places.quote: In each iteration, sample a residual for every cell, form the pseudo triangle, cumulate it and recompute the factors.
a sampled residual $r^*$ makes a pseudo value $q^*(w,d) = r^* \sqrt{m_{w,d}} + m_{w,d}$

requirements.statement: Chain ladder age-to-age factors are volume-weighted (sum of later cumulative over sum of earlier cumulative for accident years with both), and the expected incremental for a future period is the latest cumulative times the cumulative LDF minus the next LDF-based increment.

places.quote: Compute volume-weighted factors and divide the latest diagonal backwards to get the fitted incremental values.
**Project from the pseudo diagonal.** AY 2 gives $2{,}053.7 \times 0.0464 = 95.3$.

requirements.statement: For an over-dispersed Poisson distribution, variance equals the scale parameter φ times the mean.

places.quote: drawn from a [[Gamma|gamma]] with that mean and variance $\phi\, m^*_{w,d}$, where $\phi$ is the scale parameter.

requirements.statement: The ODP scale parameter φ equals the sum of squared unscaled Pearson residuals divided by (N − p), or equivalently the sum of squared standardized Pearson residuals divided by N, where N is the number of data cells and p the number of parameters.

places.quote: the scale parameter $\phi = \sum r^2/(N-p)$ with $p = 2n - 1$
$\phi$ is still calculated from the unscaled residuals, though $\sum (r^{H})^2/N$ approximates it.

requirements.statement: Process variance is incorporated in a bootstrap by simulating each future incremental claim from a process distribution (e.g., gamma or ODP) whose mean is the projected value and whose variance is φ times the mean.

places.quote: $$q_{\text{future}}(w,d) \sim \mathrm{Gamma}\left(m^{*}_{w,d},\ \phi\, m^{*}_{w,d}\right)$$

requirements.statement: A change in claims settlement rate alters the pattern of payments, raising parameter risk because historical development no longer reflects the future, and affecting process risk by changing the volatility and timing of ultimate payments.

resolution.quote: change, making historical paid factors too large
resolution.note: Loss Reserving (syllabus page) teaches that a settlement rate change makes historical development factors unrepresentative of the future, which is parameter risk (tagged Parameter Risk); the process-risk effect follows from the change in the size and timing of what is still unpaid

requirements.statement: Internal systemic risk correlation refers to correlation of risk across segments within a company, arising from shared drivers like common management, systems or economic conditions; operating units independently reduces but does not eliminate this correlation.

places.quote: *Parameter selection error* is internal systemic risk, also called model specification risk (a [[Model Risk|model risk]]), and is potentially common across claim groups (see [[Risk Margin]]).

requirements.statement: To test whether a regression coefficient is statistically significant, compare it to its standard error: the coefficient is significant if its magnitude exceeds about two standard errors (roughly a 95% test), and insignificant otherwise.

places.quote: A factor is usually wanted at least twice its standard deviation (about a 4.5% chance for a Normal when the true value is zero), or 1.65 times (about 10%).

requirements.statement: Fit the regression of incremental loss at the next age on cumulative loss to date, compute fitted values and residuals (actual minus predicted) for each accident year, and compute the sum of squared deviations of x from its mean to use in the standard error formulas.

places.quote: A **residual** is the part of an observation a fitted model does not explain: the observed value minus the [[Fitted Values|fitted value]].
$S_{jj} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{ij} - \bar{x}_j)^2$ is the centred sum of squares of predictor $x_j$

requirements.statement: In simple linear regression the standard error of the slope is s_b = sqrt(sum e_i^2 / ((n-2) sum (x_i - xbar)^2)), and the standard error of the intercept is s_a = s_b * sqrt((1/n) sum x_i^2), with n-2 degrees of freedom.

The chain ladder (Mack) model assumes that expected incremental loss in the next development period is proportional to loss to date, so testing the significance of the slope (LDF) validates this proportionality assumption.

places.quote: The first says expected emergence is proportional to losses emerged to date: a line through the origin, with the same factor for every accident year.
Future development is proportional to what has emerged.

requirements.statement: The additive (Bornhuetter-Ferguson-type) model assumes expected future incremental loss is independent of loss to date, so it is not affected by abnormally high losses to date, whereas the chain ladder multiplies losses to date by a factor and so leverages up the projected emergence.

places.quote: Age-1 emergence is about $2{,}000$ whether a year started at $700$ or $1{,}600$, which the chain ladder's proportionality cannot reproduce.
reported early is multiplied by the full CDF.

requirements.statement: Heteroscedasticity means the residuals do not share a common (constant) variance across the triangle, e.g. variance differs by development period.

places.quote: **Heteroscedasticity** is non-constant variance among a model's [[Residual|residuals]]. In a reserving model it usually means the residuals of some development periods are more variable than those of others.

requirements.statement: The GLM bootstrap assumes residuals are independent and identically distributed, so with heteroscedasticity residuals cannot be sampled freely from anywhere in the triangle; doing so biases simulated losses (some over- and some under-estimated) and misstates variability.

places.quote: The [[ODP Bootstrap Model|ODP bootstrap]] assumes the opposite, homoscedasticity: that the standardized [[Pearson Residual|Pearson residuals]] are independent and identically distributed, which is what allows a residual from one cell to be applied to any other.
The residuals are assumed independent and identically distributed, which is what [[Heteroscedasticity|heteroscedasticity]] violates; they need not be normal.

requirements.statement: To test for heteroscedasticity by development period, compare the variance/standard deviation/spread of residuals (e.g. via residual plot by development period or computed variances) across development periods; materially different variances indicate heteroscedasticity.

places.quote: - **Detecting it.** A [[Residual Plot|residual graph]] by development period shows it: the residuals in some periods spread wider than in others.
| Fan shape (spread increases) | **Heteroscedasticity** — variance is not constant |

requirements.statement: Stratified sampling adjusts for heteroscedasticity by grouping development periods whose residuals have similar variance and sampling residuals only within each group.

places.quote: *Stratified sampling* draws each group's residuals only from that group. It is simple, but a small group limits the variability of the outcomes.

requirements.statement: The hetero-adjustment approach groups residuals with similar variance, multiplies each group's standardized residuals by a hetero factor (overall standard deviation divided by group standard deviation), samples the adjusted residuals, then reverses the adjustment after sampling to avoid bias.

places.quote: $h_i$ is group $i$'s hetero-adjustment factor: the standard deviation of all the residuals over that of group $i$'s. … Dividing a sampled $r^*$ by the $h_i$ of the cell being simulated puts that group's variance back.

requirements.statement: Specification error is the internal systemic risk that the chosen model structure cannot fully capture the complexity of the insurance process (e.g., relying on a single model or missing catastrophe dynamics).
requirements.concept: Systemic Risk in Stochastic Loss Reserve Models

places.quote: **Specification error** is the inability to build a model fully representative of the insurance process.

requirements.statement: Parameter selection error is the internal systemic risk that the selected parameters, predictors and their trends do not match the true parameters and trends, for example because of limited or unrepresentative data.
requirements.concept: Systemic Risk in Stochastic Loss Reserve Models

places.quote: **Parameter selection error** arises because the model cannot adequately measure all the predictors of claim cost outcomes, or trends in them.

requirements.statement: A retrospective test compares actual emergence to the model's predicted distribution by finding the percentile of each actual outcome in the model's distribution and plotting a histogram of those percentiles.
requirements.concept: Retrospective Testing of Stochastic Reserve Models

places.quote: Each of $n$ triangles is fitted with its outcome held back, and the [[Percentile|percentile]] of the actual outcome within the model's predictive distribution is recorded.

requirements.statement: If the model is well calibrated, the percentile histogram of actual outcomes is approximately uniform; mass concentrated in low percentiles indicates the model is biased high (overstates losses), and mass concentrated in high percentiles indicates bias low.
requirements.concept: Retrospective Testing of Stochastic Reserve Models

places.quote: **Below the $45^\circ$ line throughout**: outcomes pile into the low percentiles, so the model predicts results that are **too high** (biased high).

requirements.statement: A model fit without adjustment to a short experience period containing a rare, large catastrophe event overstates expected losses in periods without such an event, and a high R-squared on thin data can reflect overfitting rather than predictive accuracy.
requirements.concept: Overfitting and Catastrophe Events in Loss Models

places.quote: Training error always falls as flexibility rises, while validation error turns up once the model starts fitting noise

Catastrophe losses are **removed** from the experience period and replaced with a long-run expected load. A five-year experience period either contains the hurricane or does not, and neither answer is the expected cost.

resolution.note: The scenario's own argument (one hurricane in five years fitted without adjustment, R-squared over 99%); what the reading supplies, specification/parameter error and reading a biased-high retrospective histogram, is on the tagged Internal Systemic Risk and PP Plot pages

requirements.statement: The log-link GLM bootstrap cannot handle negative incremental values (logs of zero or negative cells are undefined), so it needs adjustment or fails when columns or cells are negative.

places.quote: Negative incremental values use $\sqrt{|m|}$, and a negative future mean is simulated as $-\mathrm{Gamma}$ or as $\mathrm{Gamma} + 2m$.
That needs a parameter for every accident and every development period, a common $\phi$, and positive column sums; a negative column total makes the GLM fail.

requirements.statement: The GLM bootstrap has practical limitations: parameters must be re-solved at every bootstrap iteration (computationally intensive), it uses many parameters and may overfit, and it assumes iid residuals so heteroscedasticity must be adjusted for.

places.quote: The residuals must be independent and identically distributed, but need not be normal, so their skewness flows into the simulation ("semi-parametric").

The [[ODP Bootstrap Model|ODP bootstrap]] assumes the opposite, homoscedasticity: that the standardized [[Pearson Residual|Pearson residuals]] are independent and identically distributed, which is what allows a residual from one cell to be applied to any other.

requirements.statement: Convert cumulative reported loss to cumulative paid loss by subtracting case reserves, where case reserves equal the number of open claims times the average case reserve per claim at that maturity.
requirements.concept: Paid Loss from Reported Loss and Case Reserves

places.quote: $$\text{Reported Losses} = \text{Paid Losses} + \text{Case Reserves}$$
AY 2023 at $24$ months: paid to date $\$800{,}000$, case outstanding $\$500{,}000$, so reported is $\$1{,}300{,}000$.

resolution.note: Uses the question's own data: reported = paid + case, with case reserves given per open claim by maturity; converting is arithmetic on the definition of reported loss, not a reading's method

requirements.statement: Convert a cumulative paid triangle to incremental paid by differencing successive maturities in each accident year.

resolution.note: Differencing a cumulative paid triangle into incrementals is triangle arithmetic, a step of this solution's plan

requirements.statement: For a log-link GLM, the response triangle is built by taking the natural log of each incremental paid cell, which is then used to solve for the GLM parameters.

resolution.quote: Log: $g(\mu) = \ln\mu$
resolution.note: The tagged GLM page gives the log link, g(mu) = ln mu: the linear predictor is fitted to the log of each incremental mean

requirements.statement: In the log-link GLM, the log of expected incremental loss for accident year i and development period j is ln q(i,j) = alpha_i + sum of beta_k for k=2..j (beta terms cumulate over development periods), so fitted incremental = exp of that sum.

places.quote: In the log-link form of [[Using the ODP Bootstrap Model (Shapland - 2016)|Shapland's]] formula 3.7, $\alpha_1 = \beta_1 = 0$; the $\alpha_w$ adjust the level and the $\beta_d$ the development trend after the first period.
As a [[Generalized Linear Model|GLM]] with a log link it reads $\ln m_{w,d} = c + \alpha_w + \beta_d$.

requirements.statement: Reinsurers typically learn of a claim only once it pierces the reinsurance layer, so a primary claims person who reserves to a low modal value delays reporting of a potentially serious claim to the reinsurer (longer report lag).

places.quote: Claims reach the reinsurer only after the cedant has reported and assessed them. Excess claims arrive later still, once they approach the retention or a reporting threshold.

requirements.statement: Reserving a potentially serious claim to the mode (which is low because most claims are small) consistently under-reserves loss and ALAE, and reinsurance claims tend to show persistent upward development, so modal case reserves are inadequate as initial reserves.

Heterogeneous reinsurance exposures make industry statistics (e.g., Schedule P benchmarks) of limited use for reserving because they are too aggregated and do not match the reinsurer's mix of business.

places.quote: External patterns such as RAA data help but mix unlike contracts.
Two books with the same nominal line code can have very different development if one is written at higher limits.

requirements.statement: Traditional reserving methods require homogeneous data groups, but splitting heterogeneous reinsurance data into homogeneous groups reduces credibility, and aggregating dissimilar data to regain credibility is difficult.

places.quote: Credibility limits how far it can be taken.
Splitting a book finer makes each group more alike but leaves each with less data; combining groups buys volume at the price of averaging together risks that genuinely differ.

requirements.statement: Diverse coding and handling requirements for heterogeneous reinsurance business strain data coding and IT systems, causing backlogs and processing errors that hamper reserving.

resolution.quote: Every cedant and broker has different IT systems and reports. Turning their bordereaux into the format actuarial work needs is hard to do efficiently and accurately, and remains manually intensive.
resolution.note: Friedland (PDF pp.32-33, 40-41): data coding at the reinsurer and heterogeneous cedant/broker IT systems make absorbing reinsurance data hard to do efficiently and accurately, a manual process; that is the item's strain on coding and IT systems leading to delays and errors.

requirements.statement: Increased claims staffing lets adjusters set more adequate case reserves sooner, which speeds up reporting/case incurred development so that future development is lower and the pattern shortens.
requirements.concept: Changes in Claim Settlement and Case Reserve Adequacy

places.quote: **Strengthening** raises reported losses immediately, so recent age-to-age factors fall (more of the ultimate is already booked).

requirements.statement: When a change in operations shifts the development pattern, use expert opinion to override the selected link ratios or LDFs for affected diagonals or years, such as selecting a lower LDF for the latest year, rather than relying on historical averages.
requirements.concept: Incorporating Expert Opinion in Loss Development

places.quote: If a change in settlement makes an older factor wrong for recent rows, those rows share a separate factor. Its prior mean is the expert's factor, and its variance $W$ is set to reflect the strength of the opinion.
**Judgmental selection**, documented — the honest answer when the column contains a known one-off.

requirements.statement: In the chain-ladder method, applying LDFs that are higher than the true future development overstates IBNR, while applying LDFs that are too low understates IBNR.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = U_{\text{AY}} - C_{\text{AY},\,n}$$
Applying historical factors — built under weaker reserving — to a strengthened diagonal **over-states** ultimate, because the strengthening is developed a second time.

requirements.statement: Catastrophe losses have different frequency, severity and reporting/development patterns from non-catastrophe (attritional) losses, so combining them in one triangle distorts IBNR and can cause volatility, and growth in cat exposure may not yet appear in loss data.

places.quote: In **reserving**, catastrophe claims are triangulated separately: they report fast and settle in a distinctive pattern (rapid initial payment, then a long tail of disputed and litigated claims), quite unlike ordinary property claims.

resolution.quote: Catastrophe losses are estimated event by event and removed from the triangles.
resolution.note: Reinsurance Reserving (syllabus page) teaches separating catastrophe losses from the triangles and estimating them event by event, because they do not follow the attritional pattern

requirements.statement: Handle catastrophe exposure by analyzing cat and non-cat losses separately, using a catastrophe model or a cat load to estimate reserves for cat events and to reflect cat risk in IBNR.

places.quote: separate treatment of [[Large Loss|large]] and [[Catastrophe Loss|catastrophe]] claims
Catastrophe losses are **removed** from the experience period and replaced with a long-run expected load.

requirements.statement: A large claim that develops downward (favorable settlement) creates negative development in the triangle at that age, depressing the age-to-age factor for that period and the selected LDFs, so IBNR is understated if it is not adjusted.
requirements.concept: Large Claims and Outliers in Loss Triangles

places.quote: Salvage and subrogation recoveries, conservative initial case reserving, and claims closing below their reserves all produce downward development.
Lines dominated by salvage/subrogation recoveries or by conservative initial case reserving produce age-to-age factors below $1.000$

requirements.statement: Treat an anomalous large loss as an outlier by removing it from the triangle used to compute age-to-age factors, so that it does not distort the selected factors or IBNR.
requirements.concept: Large Claims and Outliers in Loss Triangles

places.quote: the actuary may exclude large claims from the initial projection, then add back a case-specific projection for the reported large claims
**Medial average** (drop high and low) — robust to a single distorted year.

requirements.statement: Used-up premium for an accident year is its rate-level adjusted (on-level) premium multiplied by the percent reported (reporting lag) at the evaluation date.

places.quote: **Used-up premium** $\text{EP}_i / \text{CDF}_i$ is the share of each year's premium "exposed" to the losses reported so far.
$P_i / \text{CDF}_i$ is the **used-up premium**, the share of the premium that the claims reported so far correspond to.

requirements.statement: The Stanard-Bühlmann (Cape Cod) expected loss ratio is total reported losses divided by total used-up premium across accident years.

places.quote: $$\text{ELR} = \frac{\sum_i C_i}{\sum_i \text{EP}_i \times \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}}$$

requirements.statement: Stanard-Bühlmann IBNR for an accident year equals premium × ELR × (1 − percent reported).

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$
$$\text{IBNR}_j = \text{ELR}_j \times P_j \times \left(1 - \frac{1}{\text{CDF}_j}\right)$$

requirements.statement: Chain ladder IBNR equals reported loss divided by percent reported, minus reported loss (i.e., reported × (1 − p)/p).

places.quote: chain ladder IBNR is its ultimate times $1 - p_t$
$$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$ … $$\text{IBNR} = U_{\text{AY}} - C_{\text{AY},\,n}$$

requirements.statement: Credibility-weight the chain ladder and Stanard-Bühlmann IBNR estimates using Z equal to a selected credibility factor multiplied by the percent reported (lag) at the starting evaluation date, with Z on chain ladder and 1−Z on Stanard-Bühlmann.

places.quote: $$\text{Estimate} = Z \times \text{Experience} + (1 - Z) \times \text{Complement}$$
BF is a **credibility weighting** in disguise: it equals $Z \, U_{\text{CL}} + (1-Z)\,U_0$ with $Z = 1/\text{CDF}$.

requirements.statement: Expected loss emergence over a period is the IBNR estimate times the incremental percent reported during the period divided by the percent unreported at the start of the period, ((p_end − p_start)/(1 − p_start)).

requirements.statement: In Bühlmann-Straub-style Bayesian credibility for a ratio such as percent recovered, VHM = (E[percent])^2-type variance of the hypothetical mean, EVPV = expected process variance, and Z = VHM/(VHM+EVPV); the estimate is Z*(data-based estimate) + (1-Z)*(prior mean).

requirements.statement: Standardized Pearson residuals in a GLM are (actual − fitted incremental loss) divided by the square root of the fitted value (scaled by a dispersion factor), and are used as the resampling pool in a bootstrap.

places.quote: **Pearson Residual** is an actual incremental loss minus its fitted value, divided by the standard deviation the model implies for that cell. For the [[Over-Dispersed Poisson Model|over-dispersed Poisson]] model the divisor is $\sqrt{m}$.
The semi-parametric bootstrap may resample Pearson, deviance or any residual whose inverse exists.

requirements.statement: Bootstrap residuals must be identically distributed (same variance) for random resampling to be valid; if residual standard deviations differ materially across groups (heteroscedasticity), the residuals must be adjusted before sampling.

places.quote: The [[ODP Bootstrap Model|ODP bootstrap]] assumes the opposite, homoscedasticity: that the standardized [[Pearson Residual|Pearson residuals]] are independent and identically distributed, which is what allows a residual from one cell to be applied to any other.
The residuals must be independent and identically distributed, but need not be normal

requirements.statement: The heteroscedasticity adjustment factor for a group is h_i = (overall standard deviation of residuals) / (standard deviation of residuals in group i), and the group's residuals are adjusted by multiplying by h_i.

places.quote: $h_i$ is group $i$'s hetero-adjustment factor: the standard deviation of all the residuals over that of group $i$'s. Multiplied by $h_i$, every group's residuals have the same standard deviation
rescale with a **hetero-adjustment** factor $h_i = \mathrm{sd}(\text{all } r)/\mathrm{sd}(r \in \text{group } i)$.

requirements.statement: When a residual is sampled and placed into a cell, first undo the sampled residual's group adjustment by dividing by the h of the cell's destination group (adjusted residual from source group divided by destination h), so the residual is on the destination group's variance level.

places.quote: Dividing a sampled $r^*$ by the $h_i$ of the cell being simulated puts that group's variance back.

requirements.statement: Sample the expected loss (a priori ultimate) for a stochastic BF by using a random number against the given cumulative distribution function of expected losses, with linear interpolation between the CDF points.

requirements.statement: The age-to-ultimate CDF is the product of the age-to-age factors (computed from the fitted or sampled cumulative triangle) and the tail factor; percent unreported/unpaid is 1 − 1/CDF.

places.quote: and $1 - 1/\text{CDF}$ the percentage unreported from the [[Development Triangle|development pattern]].
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \left(\prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1}\right) \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: The Bornhuetter-Ferguson reserve equals expected ultimate loss × (1 − 1/CDF); the total reserve is the sum over accident years, and the range of indications comes from the simulations (fitted-triangle LDFs for one, sampled-triangle LDFs for the other).

places.quote: $$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$
$$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$

requirements.statement: The Bayesian ultimate loss estimate (Meyers) is a credibility-weighted average of the chain ladder ultimate and the Bornhuetter-Ferguson ultimate: Bayesian = Z × Chain Ladder + (1 − Z) × BF.

places.quote: So the same $Z$ blends the chain ladder and BF *reserves* for the whole accident year.

requirements.statement: The credibility for the Bayesian ultimate is Z = p / (p + β·φ), where p is the percent of ultimate reported (incurred losses divided by chain ladder ultimate, i.e., 1/LDF), β is the prior distribution's rate parameter, and φ is the dispersion parameter.

places.quote: $$Z_{ij} = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{j-1} y_k}{\beta_i\,\phi + \sum_{k=1}^{j-1} y_k}$$

requirements.statement: A larger variance of the prior distribution of expected ultimate losses (smaller β) gives more credibility to the chain ladder estimate, so the Bayesian ultimate lies closer to the chain ladder ultimate. A smaller prior variance (larger β) puts the Bayesian ultimate closer to the BF ultimate.

places.quote: For a given $M_i$, a larger $\beta_i$ is a smaller prior variance and more certainty about $M_i$. That pushes $Z_{ij}$ toward $0$, which is the Bornhuetter-Ferguson method. A small $\beta_i$, a vague prior, pushes $Z_{ij}$ toward $1$, the chain ladder.
Priors with large variances reproduce the [[Chain Ladder Method|chain ladder]], and priors with very small variances reproduce Bornhuetter-Ferguson.

requirements.statement: For a gamma prior with parameters α and β, the variance is α/β², so for a given α a larger β implies a smaller prior variance.

places.quote: $$E[x_i] = M_i = \frac{\alpha_i}{\beta_i}$$ … $$\mathrm{Var}(x_i) = \frac{M_i}{\beta_i}$$
Some texts parameterize by **rate** $\beta = 1/\theta$, giving $E[X] = \alpha/\beta$.

requirements.statement: In the correlated chain ladder model, the log mean ultimate for accident year w is μ_w = α_w + β_d (with the development-period term) + ρ·(ln(incurred loss of AY w−1) − μ_{w−1}), where ρ is the correlation parameter; the ultimate is e^μ.

places.quote: Each year's log mean moves by $\rho$ times the previous year's deviation from its own log mean.

requirements.statement: The correlated chain ladder model incorporates correlation between accident years (via ρ) and has been shown (Meyers) to accurately describe the distribution of reserve outcomes.

places.quote: Meyers concludes that the CCL predicts the distribution of incurred outcomes correctly within the specified confidence level.

requirements.statement: The Bayesian method can incorporate expert opinion (an informative prior) and produces a full predictive distribution of outcomes in addition to a point estimate.

places.quote: The row parameters $x_i$ of the [[Over-Dispersed Poisson Model|over-dispersed Poisson]] model, each accident year's expected ultimate loss, are given [[Gamma|gamma]] prior distributions that carry an expert's view of the ultimate.
Bayesian models, simulated by [[Markov Chain Monte Carlo]], give the full predictive distribution of the reserves, and the prediction error is the standard deviation of that distribution.

requirements.statement: In an exponential dispersion family, θ is the canonical (location) parameter, related to the mean by θ = (b')^{-1}(μ).

places.quote: $\theta$ is the **canonical parameter**, $\phi$ the [[Dispersion Parameter]], $b(\theta)$ the cumulant function whose derivatives generate the mean and variance

requirements.statement: In an exponential dispersion family, b(θ) is the cumulant function, whose first derivative gives the mean (μ = b'(θ)) and whose second derivative determines the variance function.

places.quote: $$E[Y] = b'(\theta) = \mu, \qquad \text{Var}(Y) = a(\phi)\,b''(\theta) = \phi\,V(\mu)$$

requirements.statement: The Tweedie sub-family is obtained from the EDF by restricting the variance function to the power form V(μ) = μ^p with p ≤ 0 or p ≥ 1 (no values between 0 and 1).

places.quote: The **Tweedie Distribution** is the [[Exponential Family]] member whose variance is a power of the mean, $V(\mu) = \mu^{p}$.
The slope estimates $p$ in $V(\mu) = \mu^p$: $0$ for normal, $1$ for Poisson, $2$ for gamma, and between $1$ and $2$ for Tweedie.

requirements.statement: In the Tweedie family a larger power p gives larger variance and a heavier tail (p=2 gamma, p=3 inverse Gaussian), so a heavy-tailed exposure is modeled by choosing a larger p; the dispersion φ does not affect selection of the distribution.

places.quote: **Choosing the model** means choosing the error distribution (a larger Tweedie $p$ for a heavier tail), the covariates, the link (a multiplicative structure implies a log link) and the weights.

requirements.statement: A Tweedie GLM with p = 1 (log link) is an over-dispersed Poisson model, and its cross-classified MLE fit reproduces the standard chain ladder reserve estimates.

places.quote: Fitted as a [[Generalized Linear Model|GLM]] with a log link, it reproduces the volume-weighted [[Chain Ladder Method|chain ladder]], which is why it underlies the [[ODP Bootstrap Model|ODP bootstrap]].

- **Two GLMs reproduce the chain ladder.** The *ODP cross-classified* model has $Y_{kj} \sim \mathrm{ODP}(\alpha_k\beta_j, \phi)$ with $\sum_j \beta_j = 1$: a log link, with accident and development year as categorical covariates.

requirements.statement: Volume-weighted chain ladder age-to-age factor = sum of later-age cumulative losses divided by sum of the earlier-age cumulative losses over the same accident years.

$\hat f_k = \sum_j C_{j,k+1} / \sum_j C_{jk}$ is [[Unbiasedness|unbiased]].

requirements.statement: Estimate an accident year's ultimate loss by multiplying its latest cumulative loss by the product of the remaining age-to-age factors (cumulative development factor to ultimate).

places.quote: projects each cohort to ultimate by multiplying its latest cumulative amount by a [[Cumulative Development Factor|cumulative development factor]] derived from the historical pattern.

requirements.statement: The Stanard-Bühlmann (Cape Cod) expected loss ratio equals total aggregate reported losses divided by total used-up (adjusted) premium, where used-up premium for each accident year is adjusted premium times the percent reported (report lag).

places.quote: The ELR is estimated as total reported losses over total *used-up* (on-level, developed) premium across all years.

requirements.statement: Used-up premium (exposure) is the premium on a risk-adjusted/on-level basis (adjusted premium) multiplied by the percent of losses expected to be reported, so premium is matched to the losses reported to date.

places.quote: **Used-up premium** $\text{EP}_i / \text{CDF}_i$ is the share of each year's premium "exposed" to the losses reported so far.
$P_i / \text{CDF}_i$ is the **used-up premium**, the share of the premium that the claims reported so far correspond to.

requirements.statement: The Stanard-Bühlmann IBNR for an accident year equals adjusted premium times the ELR times (1 minus the report lag percentage).

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$
$$\text{IBNR} = \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}$$

requirements.statement: The chain ladder IBNR equals reported loss times (1/report lag minus 1), where the loss development factor is the reciprocal of the percent reported.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
The reciprocal is the **percentage reported** (or paid): $p_n = 1/\text{CDF}_n$, and $1 - p_n$ is the percentage unreported.

requirements.statement: In the credibility-weighted combination of the Stanard-Bühlmann and chain ladder methods, the weight on the chain ladder is Z equal to the selected credibility factor times the report lag, and the remaining 1 − Z goes to Stanard-Bühlmann; the IBNR is the weighted average of the two IBNR estimates.
requirements.concept: Credibility-Weighted Combination of Chain Ladder and Stanard-Bühlmann

requirements.statement: The chain ladder method is responsive to actual reported losses but is highly leveraged and unstable at immature ages with large LDFs, while Stanard-Bühlmann is stable but relies on premium/on-level adjustments and ignores emerging losses; a credibility-weighted combination is used when the actuary has partial confidence in both, giving more weight to chain ladder as the year matures.
requirements.concept: Credibility-Weighted Combination of Chain Ladder and Stanard-Bühlmann

places.quote: and at its worst at immature ages in [[Long Tail Lines|long-tail lines]], where the CDF is large and the diagonal is thin.

places.quote: Bordereau delays are one of Friedland's reasons that reinsurance reporting and payment patterns are longer than primary ones
Claims reach the reinsurer only after the cedant has reported and assessed them. Excess claims arrive later still, once they approach the retention or a reporting threshold.

Reinsurance exposures are heterogeneous (differing by product, retention, attachment point, policy terms), so data are not homogeneous and industry statistics and benchmarks are less useful for reinsurance reserving.

places.quote: a bordereau's loss detail is far less complete than the claim file behind it
Data often arrive as summary reports rather than claim detail

places.quote: For each retro adjustment it is the premium developed in that adjustment divided by the loss developed over the matching loss valuations.

requirements.statement: The formula method responds to changing retro parameters, is more stable, and captures the nonlinear, declining premium responsiveness at later adjustments, but requires hard-to-estimate parameters (e.g., tax multiplier, loss conversion factor), is more calculation-intensive, uses average factors that may not fit individual accounts, and may not reflect data trends promptly.

requirements.statement: The individual (chain ladder) reserve is R^ind = Loss × q/p, and the collective (BF-type) reserve is R^coll = Premium × ELR × q.

places.quote: $m_k$ is the **incremental loss ratio** of development period $k$: the paid claims $S_{ik}$ of that period, summed over the origin periods that have reached it, divided by those periods' premium.

places.quote: **Direct development** applies an [[Excess Loss Development Factor|excess loss development factor]] to reported excess losses.

requirements.statement: Under an exponential severity distribution, a smaller parameter (smaller mean) means limits eliminate a smaller share of losses, so limited expected values are closer to the unlimited expected value and the excess layer is a smaller portion of losses.

places.quote: Exponential$(\theta)$ | $\theta(1 - e^{-u/\theta})$ |
Capped at a [[Benefit Limit|limit]] $u$: $E[\min(X,u)] = \theta\left(1 - e^{-u/\theta}\right)$

requirements.statement: A smaller excess share of expected losses at early maturity relative to later maturity makes the excess layer more leveraged, which raises the excess-layer development factor and the estimated ultimate excess loss.
requirements.concept: Sahasrabuddhe Increased Limits and Layer Loss Development

places.quote: Layer development factors are leveraged and volatile.
Late development lands mostly above the deductible, so the LER falls with maturity ($R^L < R^L_t$), and $\text{XSLDF}^L_t > \text{LDF}_t > \text{LDF}^L_t$.

requirements.statement: In the Cape Cod method (Clark), expected prospective losses equal the ELR times the premium (exposure base).

places.quote: \hat R &= 0.70 \times 10{,}000 \times 0.40
Each fitted increment is $\mu = P \cdot \text{ELR} \cdot \Delta G$.

requirements.statement: Process variance of prospective losses equals the variance/mean ratio (sigma squared) times the expected losses.

places.quote: \mathrm{Var}_{\text{process}}(R) = \sigma^2 \sum \mu_{AY;x,y}
\text{Process} &= \sigma^2 \hat R = 50 \times 2{,}800

requirements.statement: For Cape Cod prospective losses (premium times ELR), the parameter variance equals premium squared times the variance of the ELR estimate, taken from the parameter covariance matrix (other parameters like omega and theta do not enter since prospective losses depend only on ELR).

places.quote: Parameter variance, $(\partial R)'\,\Sigma\,(\partial R)$, comes from parameters shared by every year, and does not diversify this way.
\text{Parameter} &= (10{,}000 \times 0.40)^2 \times 0.05^2

requirements.statement: Total variance of prospective losses is the sum of process variance and parameter variance; the coefficient of variation is the square root of total variance divided by the expected losses.
requirements.concept: Coefficient of Variation of Loss Estimates

places.quote: Clark adds the two, treating them as independent.
\mathrm{Var}(R) = \underbrace{E\big[\mathrm{Var}(R \mid \theta)\big]}_{\text{process}} + \underbrace{\mathrm{Var}\big(E[R \mid \theta]\big)}_{\text{parameter}}
Dividing it by the mean gives the [[Coefficient of Variation|coefficient of variation]].

requirements.statement: Process variance measures the uncertainty from the inherent randomness of the insurance loss process, while parameter variance measures the uncertainty arising from the parameters being estimated or selected rather than known true values.

places.quote: **Process risk** is the variability of actual outcomes around their expected value that would remain even if the model and its parameters were known exactly

**Parameter risk** is the uncertainty in a reserve that comes from not knowing the model's parameters: development factors, an expected loss ratio or growth-curve parameters are estimated from limited, noisy data.

requirements.statement: The Cape Cod method typically has lower parameter variance than the chain ladder (LDF) method because it uses fewer parameters (less overparameterization) and incorporates exposure/premium information.
requirements.concept: Cape Cod vs Chain Ladder Parameter Variance

places.quote: He notes that the Cape Cod method may carry somewhat more process variance than the LDF method but much less estimation error.
Replacing the ultimates with one Cape Cod ELR leaves 3 parameters, and the parameter standard deviation of the total reserve falls from $4{,}688{,}826$ to $3{,}143{,}967$

requirements.statement: The loglogistic growth curve is G(x) = x^ω / (x^ω + θ^ω), giving the expected cumulative proportion of ultimate loss paid (or reported) at age x.

places.quote: \text{Loglogistic: } G(x) = \frac{x^{\omega}}{x^{\omega} + \theta^{\omega}}

requirements.statement: With uniform accident occurrence over a year, the average age of an accident year at a valuation date is the evaluation age in months minus 6 months, and the cumulative pattern is evaluated at that average age (e.g., a 12-month evaluation uses average age 6).

places.quote: The age $x$ runs from the *average* accident date to the evaluation date, so an [[Accident Year|accident year]] evaluated $t \ge 12$ months after it starts has $x = t - 6$.

requirements.statement: When payments stop after a truncation point, the pattern is truncated: G is evaluated at the truncation age (average age at the truncation point) and the pattern is normalized by dividing G(x) by G(truncation age), so the pattern reaches 100% at truncation.

places.quote: Clark truncates at a selected age $x_T$ (240 months), using $G(x_T)/G(x)$ in place of $1/G(x)$.

requirements.statement: The Cape Cod ELR estimate is total cumulative actual loss to date divided by the sum of on-level premium times G(x) (used-up premium) across accident years, with G consistent (truncated/normalized or not) with the ultimate it applies to.

places.quote: The ELR is estimated as total reported losses over total *used-up* (on-level, developed) premium across all years.

requirements.statement: Expected incremental loss in a period for an accident year equals premium × ELR × [G(end age) − G(start age)]; for the first period the start G is 0.

places.quote: The expected increment between ages $x$ and $y$ is $\text{ULT}_{AY}[G(y) - G(x)]$ in Clark's LDF method, or $\text{Premium}_{AY} \times \text{ELR} \times [G(y) - G(x)]$ in his [[Cape Cod Method|Cape Cod]] method.

requirements.statement: The normalized (Pearson) residual is (actual incremental − expected incremental) / sqrt(σ² × expected incremental), where σ² is the scale parameter of the over-dispersed Poisson model.

places.quote: The same $\sigma^2$ scales the normalized residuals $(c - \hat\mu)/\sqrt{\sigma^2\hat\mu}$ used to check the fit.
r_{w,d} = \frac{q(w,d) - m_{w,d}}{\sqrt{m_{w,d}^{z}}}

requirements.statement: Cape Cod ultimate loss for an accident year equals paid to date plus the unpaid estimate, where unpaid = ELR × premium × [G(truncation) − G(current age)] (using the normalized pattern: ELR × premium × (1 − normalized G)).

places.quote: \text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)
\hat U_j = C_j + \text{IBNR}_j

requirements.statement: To test for calendar year effects with Mack's method, apply the test to the age-to-age development factor triangle (not the loss triangle), and within each column of factors label each factor as large (above the column median), small (below the median), or neither (equal to the median, excluded).

places.quote: In each column, factors above the [[Median|median]] are L and below it are S; with an odd count the median factor is dropped.

requirements.statement: For each calendar year diagonal, count the large and small factors and set Z_i = min(#L, #S); the test statistic Z is the sum of Z_i over all diagonals (diagonals with a single observation contribute zero/are excluded).

places.quote: $$Z_j = \min(L_j,\ S_j)$$ … A diagonal with $n \le 1$ is left out.

requirements.statement: Form a 95% confidence interval E[Z] ± 1.96·sqrt(Var(Z)) (the standard deviation is the square root of the variance) and reject the null hypothesis of no calendar year effects if Z falls outside it.

places.quote: "no calendar year effect" is rejected at 5% if $Z$ falls outside $E(Z) \pm 2\sqrt{\text{Var}(Z)}$.

requirements.statement: A sustained increase in calendar year trend raises actual losses above expected on all later diagonals, giving persistently positive residuals rather than a reversal to negative residuals.

places.quote: If the diagonals measure claims inflation, the latest ones can be projected forward ([[Separation Method]]).
**(c) Permanent.** Every future diagonal carries the higher award level, so each future cell is $10\%$ higher and the unpaid estimate is $1.1 \times 12{,}200 = 13{,}420$.

requirements.statement: An increase in case reserve adequacy raises case incurred losses in the year of the change (positive residuals) and reduces later case incurred development (negative residuals afterward) once the strengthening stops, because the reserves are already higher.

places.quote: **Strengthening** raises reported losses immediately, so recent age-to-age factors fall (more of the ultimate is already booked).

requirements.statement: An acceleration of loss payments affects paid loss development but not case incurred losses, since payments are offset by reductions in case reserves, so it would not produce calendar year residual patterns in incurred data.

places.quote: **Reported data is largely immune**, because reported losses include the case reserve whether or not the claim has closed.

A moving **disposal rate** is a [[Settlement Rate|settlement speed]] change and distorts **paid** development; a jump in **average case outstanding** is a [[Case Adequacy|case adequacy]] change and distorts **reported** development.

requirements.statement: A fitted growth curve (loglogistic or Weibull) implies a tail beyond the latest observed age, with percent emerged below 100% at the end of the data, so its development factor to ultimate exceeds 1 and can give a higher ultimate than a weighted average LDF method that has no tail factor.
requirements.concept: Clark Curve Fitting of Loss Emergence Patterns

places.quote: The curve extrapolates to infinite age, so it produces its own [[Tail Factor|tail factor]].

requirements.statement: A fitted growth curve is monotonically increasing in percent emerged, so it cannot reflect negative development (e.g., salvage and subrogation), whereas weighted average age-to-age factors can reflect it.
requirements.concept: Clark Curve Fitting of Loss Emergence Patterns

places.quote: Emergence must rise strictly from $0\%$ to $100\%$, so a line with real expected negative development, such as significant salvage recoveries, needs a different model.
Salvage and subrogation recoveries, conservative initial case reserving, and claims closing below their reserves all produce downward development.

requirements.statement: A weighted average LDF is sensitive to outlying age-to-age factors and to the weights chosen, while a curve fit smooths out spurious points in the data.

places.quote: And the pattern is smooth instead of following every random movement in the [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]].
equal weight to each year, so a small, volatile year counts as much as a large one.

requirements.statement: Advantages of the curve-fit method: it uses few parameters, which reduces parameter variance, it provides a tail beyond the observed data, it can be evaluated at any age, including mid-period, and it does not require triangle-format data.
requirements.concept: Clark Curve Fitting of Loss Emergence Patterns

places.quote: Only two parameters describe the whole pattern.

requirements.statement: Advantages of the weighted average LDF method: it is simple to calculate and explain, relies directly on the company's actual data, and can place more weight on recent diagonals or years when the pattern changes.

places.quote: uses only the most recent $k$ accident years — reduces the influence of older, potentially unrepresentative data
average (volume-weighted or simple) — responsive to a genuine change in the pattern, at the cost of credibility.

requirements.statement: The Cape Cod method has fewer parameters than the LDF method because it uses a single expected loss ratio (ELR) across all years rather than a separate ultimate for each year, and it uses exposure/on-level premium information, which reduces parameter variance and the standard deviation of ultimate losses.

places.quote: The ELR is estimated as total reported losses over total *used-up* (on-level, developed) premium across all years.

Replacing the ultimates with one Cape Cod ELR leaves 3 parameters, and the parameter standard deviation of the total reserve falls from $4{,}688{,}826$ to $3{,}143{,}967$; the total variance is cut in half.

requirements.statement: In Clark's LDF method with a curve fit, total variance includes process variance and parameter variance, which includes uncertainty in the curve parameters and the tail. A weighted average LDF method does not estimate curve parameters and so has lower parameter variance.
requirements.concept: Clark Variance of Ultimate Loss Estimates

places.quote: $\omega$, $\theta$ and the ultimates or ELR are fitted by [[Maximum Likelihood Estimation|maximum likelihood]] on [[Over-Dispersed Poisson Model|over-dispersed Poisson]] increments
where the covariance matrix $\Sigma$ comes from the inverse [[Fisher Information|information matrix]] of the [[Maximum Likelihood Estimation|maximum likelihood]] fit.
Clark adds the two, treating them as independent.

requirements.statement: Specification error is the internal systemic risk that the selected model cannot perfectly represent the underlying insurance (loss) process and so cannot accurately estimate the losses it generates.

places.quote: **Specification error** is the inability to build a model fully representative of the insurance process.

requirements.statement: Parameter selection error is the internal systemic risk that the model fails to identify or measure all predictors of future claim costs (and trends in them), so the best parameters are not used.

places.quote: **Parameter selection error** arises because the model cannot adequately measure all the predictors of claim cost outcomes, or trends in them.

requirements.statement: Data error is the internal systemic risk that an effective model cannot be fitted because data is of poor quality, lacking or not credible, or because of insufficient knowledge of the book of business.

places.quote: **Data error** comes from poor or unavailable data, or inadequate knowledge of the portfolio, including its pricing, underwriting and claims processes.

requirements.statement: In a balanced scorecard of internal systemic risk, score each risk source (specification, parameter selection, data) by whether the modeling process follows best practices: diagnostic testing, comprehensive internal and external predictors, reconciled data and consistent predictors score high; modeling heterogeneous lines together, changing predictors, and unfamiliarity with past processes or claims staff score low.

places.quote: Each indicator is scored against best practice even where best practice is not possible for the portfolio, since it is easy to be defensive about one's own models.
It is scored against best practice on a **balanced scorecard**, with each indicator rated 1 to 5, and the weighted score is mapped to a CoV.

requirements.statement: Better balanced scorecard scores (best-practice risk indicators) map to a lower coefficient of variation, because they reduce the magnitude of internal systemic risk and hence the variability of predicted losses; poor scores map to a higher CoV.

places.quote: For a single aggregated model with limited data, few predictors and heavy subjective adjustment, $20\%$ or more is readily justifiable and may be the largest source of uncertainty.

requirements.statement: A paid development to lead-date-loss (PDLD) ratio for a retro adjustment period is the expected incremental retrospective premium change in that adjustment divided by the expected incremental loss emerging in that period, i.e. premium developed per dollar of loss.

places.quote: For each retro adjustment it is the premium developed in that adjustment divided by the loss developed over the matching loss valuations.

requirements.statement: The cumulative PDLD ratio at a given adjustment is the average of the later-period PDLD ratios weighted by the expected share of loss emerging in each later period, with the denominator being the total expected loss still to emerge.

places.quote: $\text{CPDLD}_k$ averages the PDLDs from adjustment $k$ onward, weighted by the expected loss emerging in each: $\sum_{j \ge k} \text{PDLD}_j\, \Delta\%L_j \,/\, \sum_{j \ge k} \Delta\%L_j$.
$$\text{CPDLD}_k = \frac{\sum_{n \ge k} \text{PDLD}_n \, \Delta\%L_n}{\sum_{n \ge k} \Delta\%L_n}$$

requirements.statement: Loss emerging after the last allowable retro adjustment generates no additional premium, so it is included in the CPDLD denominator with a PDLD ratio of zero.
Expected future retro premium equals the cumulative PDLD ratio times the expected loss still to emerge.

places.quote: $$\text{Future premium} = \text{CPDLD} \times \text{Expected future loss emergence}$$
$$\text{Ult. premium} = P_{\text{last adj.}} + \text{CPDLD}_k \times \text{Future loss emergence}$$

requirements.statement: Expected ultimate retro premium equals the premium booked from the latest retro adjustment plus expected future premium, and the premium asset equals ultimate premium minus premium booked to date (which reflects interim return premium).

places.quote: $$\text{Premium reserve} = \text{Expected ultimate premium} - \text{Premium booked to date}$$
$$\text{Ult. premium} = P_{\text{last adj.}} + \text{CPDLD}_k \times \text{Future loss emergence}$$

requirements.statement: The PDLD (premium development to loss development) ratio at an adjustment is the incremental retrospective premium booked through that adjustment divided by the incremental loss reported through the corresponding evaluation.

places.quote: For each retro adjustment it is the premium developed in that adjustment divided by the loss developed over the matching loss valuations.

requirements.statement: The formula PDLD ratio at an adjustment equals (basic premium × tax multiplier)/reported loss plus (capped loss/reported loss) × loss conversion factor × tax multiplier, where capped loss reflects the retro maximum, minimum and per-accident limitation.

places.quote: $$\text{PDLD}_1 = \frac{\text{BPF} \times \text{TM}}{\text{ELR} \times \%L_1} + \frac{CL_1}{L_1}\,\text{LCF} \times \text{TM}$$
$$\text{PDLD}_1 = \frac{\text{BP} \times \text{TM}}{L_1} + \frac{CL_1}{L_1} \, \text{LCF} \times \text{TM}$$

requirements.statement: To diagnose a trend in empirical PDLD ratios, compare them with the formula ratio computed from the parameters of plans currently sold: if the formula ratio has not risen, the trend is not due to a change in plan parameters but to a change in actual loss experience that the formula cannot see.

places.quote: PDLDs can come from the plan parameters sold, which respond to changes in plan design, or from history, dividing booked premium by reported loss.
Teng and Perkins selected the first ratio at $1.750$, against a historical $1.460$ and a formula $1.426$. Recent quarters had trended up, which they attribute more likely to improved loss experience.

requirements.statement: Better loss experience places more loss within the retro maximum and per-accident limitation, raising the capped-loss-to-loss ratio and thus the PDLD ratio; worse experience pushes loss above the maximum and lowers the ratio.

places.quote: Later PDLDs fall well **below 1** as more of each new dollar of loss lands above a cap.
They are usually **well below 1**, as more new loss lands above the caps.

requirements.statement: Upward development in high loss layers combined with return premium in lower layers makes incremental PDLD ratios after the first adjustment fluctuate (even go negative), rather than producing a steady trend at the first adjustment.

places.quote: An individual policy quarter's historical ratio can even be negative. That happens when upward development above the limits coincides with downward development within them.

requirements.statement: Mack's volume-weighted age-to-age factor is f_k = (sum of C_{j,k+1} over accident years with both ages) / (sum of C_{j,k} over the same years), i.e., the weighted average of individual link ratios with weights C_{jk}.

places.quote: Mack estimates volume-weighted factors $\hat{f}_k = \sum_i C_{i,k+1} / \sum_i C_{i,k}$
$$f_{n \to n+1}^{\text{vol-wtd}} = \frac{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,n+1}}{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,n}}$$
$\hat f_k = \sum_j C_{j,k+1} / \sum_j C_{jk}$ is [[Unbiasedness|unbiased]].

requirements.statement: Mack's unbiased estimator of the variance parameter is alpha_k^2 = (1/(I-k-1)) * sum over j=1..I-k of C_{jk} * (C_{j,k+1}/C_{jk} - f_k)^2.

places.quote: \hat\sigma_k^{2} = \frac{1}{I-k-1}\sum_{j=1}^{I-k} C_{j,k}\left(\frac{C_{j,k+1}}{C_{j,k}} - \hat f_k\right)^{2}
\hat\alpha_k^2 = \frac{1}{I-k-1}\sum_{j=1}^{I-k} C_{jk}\left(\frac{C_{j,k+1}}{C_{jk}} - \hat f_k\right)^2

requirements.statement: In Mack's model, Var(C_{j,k+1} | C_{jk}) = alpha_k^2 * C_{jk}, so squared link-ratio deviations are weighted by the age-k amount C_{jk}.

places.quote: \mathrm{Var}(C_{i,k+1} \mid C_{i,k}) = C_{i,k}\,\sigma_k^2
\text{Var}(C_{i,k+1} \mid C_{i1}, \dots, C_{ik}) = C_{ik}\,\alpha_k^2

requirements.statement: The divisor I-k-1 in Mack's variance estimator is the number of link ratios (I-k) minus one degree of freedom lost by estimating f_k, which makes the estimator unbiased.

places.quote: The divisor $n - 1$ is the **degrees of freedom**: one is spent estimating $\mu$ by $\bar{X}$, and the deviations $X_i - \bar{X}$ sum to zero, so only $n-1$ of them are free

requirements.statement: Mack (1994) suggests approximating the distribution of the chain ladder reserve by a lognormal distribution when the standard error is large relative to the reserve (e.g., more than half), because a normal approximation can give negative values and is symmetric.

places.quote: When the [[Unpaid Claim Distribution|reserve distribution]] is rather skewed — especially once the standard error exceeds half of $R$, where a normal interval's lower limit turns negative — he fits a lognormal with the same mean and variance
When $\text{s.e.}(\hat R_i)$ exceeds about $50\%$ of $\hat R_i$, Mack recommends a [[Lognormal Distribution|Lognormal]] with the same mean and variance.

requirements.statement: For a lognormal distribution with parameters mu and sigma, the mean is exp(mu + sigma^2/2) and the variance is exp(2mu + sigma^2)(exp(sigma^2) - 1).

places.quote: $$E[X] = e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}$$ … $$\text{Var}(X) = e^{2\mu+\sigma^2}(e^{\sigma^2}-1)$$

requirements.statement: To fit a lognormal by matching moments to a given mean and standard deviation, set sigma^2 = ln(1 + (SD/mean)^2) and mu = ln(mean) - sigma^2/2.

places.quote: $\sigma^2 = \ln\!\big(1 + \text{s.e.}(R)^2/R^2\big)$ and $\mu = \ln R - \sigma^2/2$
$$\sigma^2 = \ln\!\left(1 + \mathrm{CV}^2\right)$$ … $$\mu = \ln E[R] - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2$$

requirements.statement: A percentile of a lognormal distribution is found as exp(mu + z*sigma), where z is the corresponding standard normal percentile.

places.quote: Its $p$-th percentile is then $R_p = e^{\mu + z_p\sigma}$.
its $z$-[[Percentile|percentile]] is $\hat R_i\exp(z\sigma_i - \sigma_i^2/2)$

requirements.statement: When combining several ODP bootstrap models, the weighted best estimate of unpaid claims is formed by applying the actuary's selected weights by accident year to each model's results, so each accident year uses only the models given weight in that year.

places.quote: Run several bootstrap models (paid and incurred chain ladder, BF, Cape Cod, GLM) and weight them by year to get a best-estimate *distribution*.
Several models are weighted by accident year into a best-estimate distribution, which is Shapland's answer to [[Model Risk|model risk]] and a basis for a [[Range of Indications|range]].

requirements.statement: The weighted range of total unpaid claims is found by taking, for each accident year, the lowest and highest mean among the models given weight in that year, then summing the minimums and the maximums across accident years.

places.quote: The **weighted range** uses, for each year, only the models given weight in that year. … A is $[100, 110]$ and B is $[700, 760]$, so the total is $[800, 870]$.

requirements.statement: The modeled range of total unpaid claims is the range from the lowest to the highest total mean unpaid among all models used, where each model's total is the sum of its accident-year means.

places.quote: The **modeled range** spans the means of every model used anywhere.

requirements.statement: A model counts as used in the modeled range if it receives at least some weight for any accident year, even if its weight is zero in other years.

places.quote: The modeled range's top end is set by the paid chain ladder on AY B, a model the actuary gave *no* weight for that year.

requirements.statement: The weighted range is narrower than the modeled range because it ignores, year by year, models given no weight, making it a more representative view of uncertainty around the actuarial central estimate.

places.quote: It is the more representative view of uncertainty in the actuarial central estimate.

requirements.statement: Inuring reinsurance applies in a specified order: a cover that inures to the benefit of another is applied first, and the later cover applies to losses net of the earlier cover's recoveries.

places.quote: **Order matters.** Covers inure in a stated sequence. Typically per-occurrence excess comes off first, then the quota share applies to what remains, and the stop-loss applies last to protect the final net result.
Order matters too: a surplus share may *inure* to the benefit of a per-risk or catastrophe cover, which then applies to what the cedant has left after it.

requirements.statement: An excess per occurrence reinsurance cover cedes the portion of each occurrence loss above the attachment point, up to the limit: min(limit, max(loss - attachment, 0)); for paid losses the same formula is applied to the paid amount on the occurrence.

places.quote: $$Y = \min\left(\max(X - R,\, 0),\; L\right)$$
$$\text{Ceded}_{\text{XS}} = \min\left(\max(X - R,\,0),\; L\right)$$
$$\text{Ceded}_{\text{XOL}} = \min\!\left(\max(X - R,\, 0),\, L\right)$$

requirements.statement: A quota share treaty cedes a fixed percentage of the losses (ultimate and paid) that reach it, after any inuring covers.

places.quote: the reinsurer takes a fixed percentage $a$ of the premium and of every loss (usually including ALAE) on a defined book.
$$\text{Ceded}_{\text{QS}} = c \times \text{Gross}$$
$$\text{Ceded}_{\text{QS}} = a \times X$$

requirements.statement: An aggregate stop-loss cover cedes the amount by which retained losses exceed the stated cap, max(retained loss - cap, 0), applied separately to ultimate and to paid losses.

places.quote: $$Y = \min\left(\max(S - A,\, 0),\; L_A\right)$$
$$\text{Ceded}_{\text{Agg}} = \min\left(\max(S - A,\,0),\; L_A\right)$$

requirements.statement: Unpaid loss equals ultimate loss minus paid loss, so ceded unpaid equals ceded ultimate minus ceded paid, and equals gross unpaid minus net unpaid.

places.quote: $$\text{Ceded unpaid} = \text{Gross unpaid} - \text{Net unpaid}$$
$$\text{Net Unpaid} = \text{Gross Unpaid} - \text{Ceded Unpaid}$$
$$\text{Unpaid} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Paid to date}$$

requirements.statement: On a quota share treaty, losses and premiums are shared at one fixed percentage from the ground up, so age-to-age factors for gross, ceded and net losses are identical.

places.quote: For reserving, ceded losses are a scalar multiple of gross and develop on the gross pattern, unlike [[Excess of Loss]] cessions.
Under **quota share**, ceded is a fixed share $c$ of gross, so the ceded triangle is a scalar multiple of the gross one and develops identically.

requirements.statement: A surplus share treaty cedes a different percentage of each risk depending on the policy limit relative to the retained line, so its gross, ceded and net age-to-age factors differ, though less than between proportional and non-proportional reinsurance.

places.quote: **Surplus Share** is a proportional treaty, common on property, in which the percentage ceded varies by risk.
**Surplus share** — cedes the portion of each policy's limit above the cedant's retention, so the cession percentage varies by policy.

requirements.statement: A risks-attaching treaty covers policies incepting during its term, so a change in its ceded percentage applies by the policy year of the underlying risks rather than by accident date, complicating ceded estimation when gross losses are analyzed by accident year.

places.quote: When the percentage changes, it follows the *policy* year on a risks-attaching treaty and the *accident* year on a losses-occurring-during treaty.
When a [[Quota Share|quota share]]'s ceded percentage changes, on an RA treaty the change follows the [[Policy Year|policy year]] of the underlying risks, not the accident year.

requirements.statement: Stop-loss reinsurance typically applies after all other reinsurance, so other covers inure to its benefit and it protects the ceding company's net result.

places.quote: **Order matters.** Covers inure in a stated sequence. Typically per-occurrence excess comes off first, then the quota share applies to what remains, and the stop-loss applies last to protect the final net result.

requirements.statement: The defining characteristic of treaty reinsurance is that the reinsurer does not underwrite individual risks; it accepts all business within the treaty terms, including policies not yet written, and so bears the risk of adverse selection from the cedant's underwriting.

places.quote: The reinsurer accepts business it has not underwritten risk by risk, so it shares the results of the cedant's underwriting
[[Treaty Reinsurance|treaty]] (a whole portfolio, ceded automatically) or [[Facultative Reinsurance|facultative]] (one risk, underwritten on its own)

requirements.statement: In facultative reinsurance the reinsurer may underwrite each submitted risk individually, which mitigates adverse selection.

places.quote: Contrast [[Facultative Reinsurance]], where each risk is offered, underwritten and priced on its own, and the reinsurer may decline it.
The cedant offers the risk, and the reinsurer underwrites and prices it on its own and is free to accept or decline.

requirements.statement: Under a surplus share treaty, the ceded proportion of each policy is (policy limit - retained line) / policy limit, and this proportion applies to every loss on that policy; policies with limits at or below the retained line cede nothing.

places.quote: s(V) = \frac{\min\left(\max(V - R,\, 0),\; N R\right)}{V}
The cedant keeps up to a fixed amount of each risk, its retained line, and cedes the part of the insured value above it, up to the treaty's number of lines.

requirements.statement: A surplus share treaty is a proportional cover, so losses are shared pro rata (even losses below the retained line are partly ceded when the limit exceeds the line), unlike excess of loss which cedes only the part of a loss above the retention.
requirements.concept: Proportional vs. Excess of Loss Reinsurance

places.quote: Once the risk's share is fixed by its size, the reinsurer pays that share of every loss on it, however small.
Once that is fixed, the reinsurer pays its share of every loss on the risk, however small.

requirements.statement: Aggregate excess of loss (stop-loss) reinsurance generally applies to all or part of the cedant's net retention, so the cedant's other reinsurance inures to the benefit of the aggregate cover.

places.quote: Covers inure in a stated sequence. Typically per-occurrence excess comes off first, then the quota share applies to what remains, and the stop-loss applies last to protect the final net result.
